Baby & Child

4 Month Old Milestones: Skills to Expect at 4 Months

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

By 4 months, most babies smile on their own to get your attention, chuckle, coo back when you talk, hold their head steady without support, bring their hands to their mouth, and push up onto their forearms during tummy time. These skills come from the CDC and AAP milestone checklist, which describes what at least 75 percent of babies can do by this age. Babies vary, and missing one item is rarely a crisis. This guide walks through each area and the few signs that deserve a call to your pediatrician.

What most babies do by 4 months

Milestone checklists can feel like a test, so it helps to know what they actually measure. The checklist most pediatricians in the United States use, published by the CDC with the American Academy of Pediatrics, lists skills that at least 75 percent of babies show by a given age. In other words, these are things most 4 month olds can already do, not a bar your baby must clear on the exact day they turn four months. Babies work on skills in bursts, and a baby who seems quiet in one area is often busy practicing another.

At 4 months the checklist covers four areas. Social skills, like smiling at you on purpose. Language, like cooing and answering your voice with sounds. Cognitive skills, like studying their own hands. And movement, like steady head control and swatting at toys. This guide walks through each area, plus feeding, sleep, and simple ways to play. It also covers the short list of signs that call for a conversation with your pediatrician. If you want the wider month by month picture, that lives in our general baby milestones guide. This page stays focused on month four.

Social and language: smiles, chuckles, and coos

By 4 months, most babies smile on their own to get your attention, not just in response to your smile. Many chuckle when you play with them, a short giggle rather than a full belly laugh. Bigger laughs usually arrive in the weeks and months that follow, and both patterns are normal. Your baby may also look at you, wiggle, or make sounds to keep your attention once they have it. This is early conversation. The back and forth matters more than the sounds themselves, so pause after you speak and give your baby a turn to answer.

Language at this age is cooing: soft, stretched vowel sounds like ooo and aah. Most 4 month olds make sounds back when you talk to them and turn their head toward your voice. You do not need flashcards or special programs to help this along. Narrate what you are doing while you change a diaper or unload groceries, use a warm, musical tone, and copy the sounds your baby makes back to them. Hearing matters here too. If your baby does not seem to respond to your voice or startle at sudden sounds, mention it at the next checkup rather than waiting.

Movement: head control, reaching, and tummy time

Head control is the headline skill of this age. Most babies hold their head steady without support by around 4 months when you carry them or hold them upright, after months of gradual strengthening. On the floor, most can push up onto their forearms during tummy time and hold a toy when you place it in their hand. You will also see swinging or swatting at dangling toys, and hands finding the mouth again and again. Hands to mouth is not only a hunger sign. It is one of the first ways babies soothe themselves and explore the world.

Reaching is clumsy at first, and that is expected. Lay your baby on their back under a play gym, or hold a soft toy just within reach, and let them bat at it. Keep tummy time short and frequent: a few minutes, several times a day, while your baby is awake and you are watching. Some babies also begin rolling around this age. Rolling timelines and the safety changes that come with them are covered in our guide to when babies roll over. Until you have read it, play it safe: never leave your baby alone on a raised surface like a bed or changing table, even for a moment.

Feeding and sleep at 4 months

Feeding stays simple at this age. Breast milk, formula, or a mix covers everything your baby needs, and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends holding off on solid foods for now. Most babies start solids closer to 6 months, when readiness signs appear, and our starting solids guide covers those signs when you get there. A classic 4 month cognitive milestone shows up at mealtimes: your baby opens their mouth when hungry at the sight of the breast or a bottle. Formula fed babies often take roughly 4 to 6 ounces per feeding every 3 to 5 hours, while breastfed babies nurse on demand, often every 3 to 4 hours during the day.

Most 4 month olds sleep about 12 to 16 hours in every 24, counting naps. Night sleep often starts to consolidate into longer stretches, and many babies settle into three or four naps a day, though the exact pattern varies widely from baby to baby. Keep the safe sleep basics steady: on the back, in a bare crib or bassinet, with no loose blankets or pillows. If sleep suddenly falls apart around this age, you may be meeting the well known 4 month sleep regression, which we explain in our sleep regressions guide. A rough sleep patch at 4 months is common and usually temporary.

Easy play, and when to call the pediatrician

Play at 4 months can be plain and short. Hold your baby in front of a mirror and let them study the face there. Offer one toy at a time for reaching practice. Talk through your day in ordinary words, read a board book, sing the same song at the same point in your routine. At this age repetition is comfort, not boredom, so a familiar game teaches more than a rotating pile of new toys. If it helps you keep track, note new skills, questions, and checkup dates in the BeMama app so they are ready for the 4 month visit.

Call your pediatrician if, by around 4 months, your baby does not coo or make sounds back, does not hold their head steady when supported upright, does not bring hands to the mouth, does not watch or swat at toys, or does not smile at people. Also call if your baby loses a skill they once had, at any age. None of these signs is a diagnosis. They are simply the agreed points where a closer look is worthwhile, and support helps most when it starts early. Trust your gut too. You know your baby's ordinary better than any checklist does.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC milestones describe skills that most children can do by a particular age across social, language, thinking, and movement domains. They support observation and conversation but do not replace standardized developmental screening.

Individual skills vary, but caregiver concern matters. Missing several expected skills, losing a skill, or a difference in movement, communication, hearing, or vision should be discussed promptly.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to preserve dated observations, growth, activities, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot label development as normal or delayed.

When to seek help

Contact your child’s healthcare professional whenever you are concerned or notice loss of a skill. Seek urgent care for an acute change, breathing difficulty, loss of responsiveness, or seizure-like activity.

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Most 4 month olds smile for attention, chuckle, coo back at you, and hold their head steady.
  • Milestone checklists describe what at least 75 percent of babies do by an age, not a pass or fail test.
  • Breast milk or formula covers all nutrition now; most babies start solids closer to 6 months.
  • Expect about 12 to 16 hours of sleep in every 24, naps included, with night sleep starting to consolidate.
  • Call your pediatrician about no cooing, a wobbly head when upright, no hands to mouth, no interest in toys, or any lost skill.

Frequently asked questions

What should a 4 month old be doing?

Most 4 month olds smile on their own to get attention, chuckle, coo back when you talk, hold their head steady without support, bring hands to their mouth, hold a toy placed in the hand, and push up onto their forearms in tummy time. These come from the CDC checklist of skills at least 75 percent of babies show by this age. A baby can be missing one or two and still be developing typically, so bring questions to the 4 month checkup rather than comparing with other babies.

When do babies laugh?

Many babies begin to chuckle by around 4 months, and fuller belly laughs often follow over the next month or two. Early laughter usually shows up during play, like gentle bouncing, silly faces, or peekaboo. If your baby smiles and coos but is not laughing yet, that is well within the normal range. Mention it to your pediatrician if your baby is not smiling at people or making sounds back by 4 months.

When do babies hold their head up?

Most babies hold their head steady without support by around 4 months. Head control builds gradually from birth: brief lifts in the early weeks, a 45 degree lift by around 2 months, and a steady upright head by around 4 months. Regular tummy time while your baby is awake and watched helps build the neck and shoulder strength behind it. If your baby's head still flops or wobbles when held upright at 4 months, bring it up with your pediatrician.

How much should a 4 month old eat?

A 4 month old still needs only breast milk or formula, with formula fed babies often taking roughly 4 to 6 ounces per feeding every 3 to 5 hours and breastfed babies nursing on demand, often every 3 to 4 hours during the day. Appetite varies from baby to baby and day to day, so watch cues like opening the mouth at the sight of the breast or bottle and turning away when full. Steady weight gain and plenty of wet diapers matter more than exact ounces. Your pediatrician tracks growth at each visit and can confirm your baby is on course.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
